title: Savitri and Satyavan
hook: the last gift, Satyavan's life given back, and a long walk home through the dark
carry: a walk home through the dark

segments.voice: Yesterday: sat, the good. Three gifts from Death, sight, a kingdom and sons, and every one for someone else. Your line was ask a favor on someone else's behalf.
screen: `SAVITRI AND SATYAVAN.` · `THREE GIFTS, ALL GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Ask once more, says Death. Savitri is still on the road behind Yama, still talking. And this time she asks for something for herself. Let me have sons, she says, sons of my own, born of Satyavan. Yama grants it. So be it. She keeps walking, and keeps speaking about the good. A gift has now been given that can only come true one way. And the noose in Yama's hand is still closed.
screen: `ASK ONCE MORE.` → `SONS, BORN OF SATYAVAN.` → `SO BE IT.`

segments.voice: It's easy to hear this as a clever trap: Death says yes too fast and gets caught. In the epic it reads more like a conversation won. Savitri speaks again about the good, how they keep to the truth and hold the world up, and Yama is pleased once more. Ask for something beyond compare, he says. Savitri asks plainly. The gift you gave me can't happen without my husband. Without him I don't want happiness, or heaven, or even my own life. Let Satyavan live. And Yama loosens the noose. He gives Satyavan back, blesses them both with a long life together, and goes on his way. Savitri returns to the clearing and takes her husband's head into her lap again. Satyavan opens his eyes like a man waking from a long sleep. Why didn't you wake me? Where's the dark one who was dragging me away? It's night now, the forest full of sounds, and he's frightened for his parents. So Savitri ties up her hair, helps him up, picks up his axe, and they walk home in the dark, his arm over her shoulder. At the hermitage, his father has his sight back; the old couple have been searching, and the hermits have been telling them their son must be alive. Savitri tells them everything. And this is why the sage Markandeya told the story at all. Yudhishthira had asked him whether any woman had been as devoted as Draupadi. Like Savitri, Markandeya says, Draupadi will save you all.
screen: `A CONVERSATION WON, NOT A TRAP.` · `WITHOUT HIM I DON'T WANT HEAVEN.` · `WAKING, AND THE WALK HOME.` · then, large: `DRAUPADI WILL SAVE YOU ALL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who is still here with you, someone you can call or sit beside or walk home with, and let their face come clear. Breathe in and notice that they're here; breathe out and let gladness fill the breath, and if someone you've lost comes to mind instead, hold them kindly too. If you pray, give thanks for them in your prayer.
Vara, a boon, the gift Yama kept offering Savitri on the road. A wife who talked with Death until he gave her husband back, and a walk home through the dark. Today's word.
Your line: a walk home through the dark. She carried the axe, and he leaned on her. Eight hundred days now.

howItsDone: Markandeya ends the story by turning back to Yudhishthira's question about Draupadi; outside the epic, some married women honor Savitri on Vat Savitri with a fast and threads tied around a banyan tree.

chat.meaning: Each of Savitri's speeches on the good pleased Yama. At last he offered a gift beyond compare, and she asked for Satyavan's life.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva (Markandeya's story of Savitri): the fourth boon; Savitri's last speech; Satyavan restored; the walk home; Dyumatsena's sight; Markandeya's conclusion about Draupadi

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli the sequence: boon of sons for Savitri by Satyavan granted; a further speech; Yama asks her to choose an incomparable boon; she asks for Satyavan's life, saying she desires neither happiness, heaven, prosperity nor life without him.
Ganguli gives the number of sons and the length of the life Yama grants; omitted under the claims rule.
'Some retellings make this a clever trap' is a soft claim about popular tellings; a Keeper may prefer to cut it.
Confirm the walk home details: she binds her hair, carries the axe, supports him; the hermits reassure Dyumatsena; his sight is restored before they arrive.
The restoration of Dyumatsena's kingdom happens the next morning in the epic and is not narrated here.
Confirm that Yudhishthira's question to Markandeya concerned a woman as devoted as Draupadi, and Markandeya's closing line that Draupadi will save them.
